Maladaptive Strategies.value: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

vignette: Tariq remembered the night not as a single story, but as sharp, disconnected fragments that did not quite fit together. He recalled the weight of the man's hand on his shoulder, the sudden rush of blood to his chest, and the way the assailant's eyes had narrowed before the strike. The assault had unfolded during the height of the afternoon heat, his shirt growing heavy and damp, his own pulse hammering against his ribs. He could feel the salted tang of his perspiration, and he was certain that the man's gaze had carried a quiet, assessing threat. When he tried to explain what happened to his wife, Layla, or to the intake physician, he would start with the porch, mention the sound of the gate, but then lose the thread entirely, his words scattering like dust. The memory never felt fully his; it sat in his chest like something that belonged to a stranger, yet demanded his attention. In the weeks that followed, his body kept watch. Whenever his heart began to race or pound, even while he was merely kneeling in the irrigation ditch mending a drip line, Tariq would freeze, certain that the old threat was returning. He grew hyperaware of scents on the air. The familiar smell of his own sweat after morning chores triggered a tightness in his throat, a quiet alarm that the assailant was near. He noticed it most when the other farmhands gathered near the equipment shed; their movements, their quiet glances, made him certain they were assessing him, watching for weakness. He had come to believe that a suspicious look from a man could unravel the careful peace he had built. His scores on the intake assessment rested at seventy-six, a number that confirmed what he had been carrying, yet the clinical label felt distant against the lived reality of his own breath and his own eyes. Tariq did not sit still through this period. He threw himself into the work, driving the tractors, repairing fences, and tending the crops long after the sun dipped below the horizon. He kept his mind occupied by the rhythm of tasks, but he also kept careful account of the calendar. When the anniversary of the assault approached, he found himself avoiding the date entirely, rescheduling meetings, taking side roads home, and slipping past the quiet moments that might summon the memory. The months accumulated, and his routine hardened into a practiced pattern. He would return to the kitchen late, his shirt heavy with the day's heat, and stare at the wall, his mind cycling through the same calculations of how to get even, how to restore what was taken. The rumination about revenge moved through him alongside the bodily alarms and the social wariness, each occupying its own space in his days. Now, at fifty-five, Tariq stands on the edge of his property, watching the fence line where the assault had occurred. The land stretches wide and familiar, yet the triggers remain sharp. He feels his pulse quicken as he walks past the equipment shed, catches the familiar tang of his own perspiration, and notes the way the delivery drivers and neighbors sometimes watch him from a distance. He has not asked for a cure, only for a way to hold the pieces without losing himself. What brought him to seek help was not a single breakdown, but the quiet accumulation of dates avoided, the relentless working, the heavy breaths in his own chest, and the unspoken certainty that the man who struck him was still out there, waiting. He hopes to learn how to carry the memory without it carrying him, and to finally finish the story he has been trying to tell.
